fact: Djibouti Telecom says DARE1 has been operational since 2021, linking Djibouti City with Bosaso and Mogadishu in Somalia and Mombasa in Kenya, 36 Tbit/s over three fibre pairs.
ITWeb reports DARE1 currently links Djibouti City with Bosaso and Mogadishu in Somalia and Mombasa in Kenya, 36 Tbit/s over three fibre pairs. (no in-service date given; article dated 2025-09-01).
TechAfrica News reports DARE1 already links Djibouti, Somalia and Kenya (no in-service date given; article dated 2025-09-01).
Wingu Africa says its two Djibouti facilities give access to 12 operational submarine cables, with more planned; no cable names or separate landing stations given for those cables.

Djibouti Telecom operates two landing stations: YAC A (AAE1, ADEN-DJIBOUTI, SEACOM, SMW3, DARE1) and Haramous (EIG, EASSy, SMW5), 8 submarine systems in service, plus terrestrial cables to Ethiopia and Somalia.

fact: Djibouti Telecom's new Ras Dika (Ras Dika CLS) landing station is described as a neutral digital port providing open-access cable landing service to submarine cable operators; announced fully operational on 7 August 2023.

La Nation's Djibouti Telecom profile says its network comprises seven international submarine cables and two terrestrial cables (Djibouti-Somalia and Djibouti-Ethiopia); landing stations are not named, the figures read as stale boilerplate (mentions 'two new cables for 2021'), and the article gives no date for the count so its publication date is used.

La Nation states Djibouti Telecom, created 20 September 1999, holds the monopoly of national and international telecommunications across Djibouti, under laws of 1998 and 2004; the statement is in the present tense of a January 2026 article.

SubTel Forum reports the DARE1 submarine cable, operational since 2021 with 36 Tbps on three fibre pairs, links Djibouti City with Bosaso and Mogadishu in Somalia and then Mombasa, Kenya, with partners Hormuud Telecom, Somtel International and Telkom Kenya.

fact: Djibouti Telecom's own page states DARE1 is its regional subsea cable and that the current DARE1 network connects Djibouti, Somalia and Kenya, with the trunk station at Mombasa (Nyali).

IsDB's project record (IATI) states the DARE-1 submarine cable, about 3,000 km linking Djibouti to Tanzania and other East African countries and financed by a US$38.8m IsDB loan to Djibouti Telecom, became operational in 2021.

DataCenterDynamics (2026-07-09) reports the original Seacom cable, launched in 2009, runs from Egypt through the Red Sea to Djibouti before branching west to India and south to South Africa, so Djibouti is on the route.

fact: Per wearetech.africa, Prime Minister Abdoulkader Kamil Mohamed said in his March 2026 general policy statement that Djibouti has 14 submarine cables; no cable or landing station is named.

SONNA reports Finance Minister Ilyas Moussa Dawaleh said at the 2026-09-03 national AI forum that twelve submarine cables currently land in Djibouti, with three more in process; no cable or station is named.

DCD states Djibouti City is a landing station for several cable systems including 2Africa, Seacom, Sea-Me-We-6, AAE-1 and DARE (Djibouti Africa Regional Express), all at the one city (not recorded as independent).
ITWeb Africa describes Djibouti Telecom as anchoring a submarine cable hub linking multiple global systems and Djibouti's 'submarine cable gateways'; no cable named.
TechCabal says Djibouti has landing points for 12 major submarine cables, including the 45,000 km 2Africa system; no landing stations named; date is the article's publication date.

fact: Wingu's release of 2 June 2025 says its two Djibouti facilities give access to 12 operational submarine cables, the second site hosting the country's first integrated cable landing station and data centre; stations not otherwise named.

Wingu describes itself as carrier-neutral and says its Djibouti cable landing station and data centre serve customers including telecom and content providers and hyperscalers, who obtain cable access there.
African Business says Djibouti is home to ten submarine cables plus terrestrial cables; the cables come ashore at four monitored self-sufficient stations (not named).
Djibouti Telecom says it has invested over $200m in undersea cables and sells connectivity to operators in Ethiopia, Somalia and Kenya, and to more than 60 ISPs in 90 countries.

AfriFiber's CEO says it is a customer of Djibouti Telecom with no alternative for international connectivity; the article calls Djibouti Telecom unrivalled there and Blue Raman at TO7 the first credible alternative.

Djibouti Telecom's own overview states 10 operational submarine cable systems (3 more under construction) connect Djibouti internationally; individual cables and landing stations other than its Ras Dika cable landing station building are not named; the page's date is its published date and counts are rolling.

The IsDB-financed project (US$16.8m, completed with an activity end date of 2016-12-30) financed the AAE-1 submarine cable connecting Djibouti to international broadband infrastructure, recipient Djibouti Telecom; the document does not state a go-live date, so the date is project completion.
Telecom Review Africa states that Djibouti's cable landing stations remain gatekept by a single state-owned operator, despite hosting one of the continent's highest concentrations of cable landings.

Fondazione Med-Or states Djibouti is crossed by 12 submarine cables, six of them linked to Italy, and that the country carries about 18% of data on international cables; a landing station for the cables is named but not the cables.
RTD reports the TO7 park's submarine cable landing station, with room for up to 5 cables, was put into service on 25 November 2024 and serves as the landing platform for a Google cable.
La Nation says Djibouti has a privileged position on international digital routes with several submarine cables.
The French Treasury note says nine submarine cables are connected to Djibouti's coast, with three more expected in 2025 and one in 2026.
We are Tech says Djibouti is currently connected to nine submarine fibre-optic cables; landing stations are not named.
